[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p47#2/r11] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · مقاتل وقطرب وابن كيسان | reports | They take laʿalla causally, meaning “so that”: worship God so that you may attain mindfulness; a poem is cited to show this usage.

[RAZI-FULL:v2p74#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Rāzī introduces the following verses as an argument establishing divine unity, prophethood, and resurrection.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | After describing believers, unbelievers, and hypocrites, God shifts from speaking about them to addressing them directly, an iltifāt also seen in 1:5. | mentions 1:5
[RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Direct address stirs and moves the hearer more than continuing to speak about that person in the third person.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The shift honors and draws the addressee near: after initially making the Messenger an intermediary, God now addresses the person without an intermediary.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The move from third to direct address suggests that a servant engaged in worship is continually ascending.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because the earlier verses narrated their condition and these verses impose difficult commands, God’s direct personal address gives relief and makes the burden pleasant.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · علقمة والحسن | reports | ʿAlqama and al-Ḥasan say that Qur’anic addresses “O people” are Meccan, while “O you who believe” is Medinan.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p75/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · القاضي | rejects | Al-Qāḍī accepts that distinction if it rests on transmitted reports, but rejects deriving it merely from the larger number of believers in Medina: believers may be addressed as people, and unbelievers may be commanded to worship just as believers are told to persist and increase in worship.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Ay connects the vocative to a noun bearing the definite article, just as dhū and alladhī connect generic nouns to descriptions and definite nouns to clauses; ay is ambiguous and needs a noun or equivalent adjective to specify it.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The vocative particle governs ay, while the following noun is its adjective, as in “O Zayd, the courteous”; unlike Zayd, ay cannot stand independently and therefore remains joined to its adjective and described noun.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The inserted attention particle reinforces the call and compensates for the genitive construction expected with ay.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The emphatic formula is frequent in the Qur’an because its commands, prohibitions, promises, threats, and momentous histories must awaken listeners who are heedless.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76#3/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī holds that a definite plural denotes the whole class; al-Ashʿarī, al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr, and Abū Hāshim dispute this, while emphasis and unrestricted exception support generality. | mentions 15:30
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76#3/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The direct address covers all people present at the time, but face-to-face speech does not directly address people who do not yet exist.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76#3/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Later generations are included by separate, mass-transmitted evidence in Muhammad’s religion, which extends these commands to everyone until the Day of Resurrection.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76#3/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Taken by genus semantics alone, the command to worship is discharged by performing one instance, since that instance brings the worship genus into existence.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76#3/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī nevertheless takes every worship act to be commanded: worship as worship is the fitting cause of the command, since it expresses glorification and submission to God.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Words normally denote linguistic or nonlinguistic things; the vocative particle is different, functioning as an act that draws attention rather than denoting another thing.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | “O Zayd” cannot mean “I call Zayd”: the latter is a truth-apt report, does not itself make Zayd the addressee, may be spoken to a third party, and reports rather than performs the call.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p76/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Though names are strongest and particles weakest, a name can join a particle in calling; by analogy, a human can serve the transcendent Lord through invocation and humble supplication. | mentions 2:30, 7:23, 40:60

[RAZI-FULL:v2p77/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · قائل | reports | An objector says unbelievers cannot be commanded to know God: if commanded while ignorant they cannot recognize the divine command, and if commanded after knowing Him the knowledge would already exist.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p77/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · قائل | reports | The objector infers that unbelievers cannot be commanded to worship, because worship before knowing God is impossible and worship afterward depends on an impossible command to acquire knowledge.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p77/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · قائل | reports | The objection also excludes believers as addressees: they already worship God, so commanding them to worship would command an accomplished act.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p77/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · من الناس | reports | One reply says worship is conditional on prior knowledge, just as zakāt is conditional on owning the minimum threshold; these proponents regard knowledge as necessary.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p77/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · من لم يقل بذلك | reports | Those who reject that reply infer that knowledge is not self-evident: commanding worship also commands its prerequisite, knowledge, as purification, obtaining water, and seeking a deposit must precede their acts.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p77/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | On this reasoning, an unbeliever can be addressed with worship, provided that he first believes and then performs worship.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p77/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · قائل | reports | A remaining objection says commanding the acquisition of knowledge is impossible; Rāzī refers the full issue to works on legal theory and argues the objection need not apply to other attributes.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p78/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | To avoid treating believers as commanded to do what is already done, Rāzī reads the command as requiring continued or increased worship; added worship is still worship.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p78/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · منكرو التكليف | reports | Opponents of divine obligation argue that equal motives make choosing an act impossible, while unequal motives make one option inevitable and the other impossible; either way, the command exceeds capacity.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p78/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · منكرو التكليف | reports | They argue that divine foreknowledge makes the commanded act either inevitable, impossible, or unknown to God; the first two defeat the command and the last attributes ignorance to God.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p78/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · منكرو التكليف | reports | They deny a benefit in obligations: God cannot benefit from worship, while any benefit to people could be granted directly without hardship, making the hardship purposeless.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p78/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · منكرو التكليف | reports | They say people do not create their own actions; if God has already created an act in a person, ordering it is redundant, and if not, the order asks for the impossible.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p78/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · منكرو التكليف | reports | They argue that obligations aim to purify the heart, so outward duties should lapse when they obstruct constant absorption in knowing God; jurists and analogists should follow rationalized rulings over appearances.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p78/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Rāzī answers the first three objections that their proponents must adopt the contradictory duty to believe that no duties exist.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p78/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī’s theological reply is that everything God does is permissible, including imposing what people call an impossible burden, because God is creator and owner.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p78/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The general command is qualified for those without understanding or capacity, including children, the insane, the unaware, the forgetful, and those unable to act. | mentions 2:233
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | After commanding worship, the verse adduces the creation of the accountable people and their predecessors as evidence for the Creator’s existence.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79#2/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Its proofs reach the highest strength because they are arranged with certainty from certain premises.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Rāzī says the verse establishes that God is known through rational inquiry and inference; he rejects the Ḥashwiyya claim that pursuing this science is an innovation.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | First reason for theology’s superiority: a science is nobler when its subject is nobler, and God’s essence and attributes are the noblest objects of knowledge.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Second reason: religious sciences outrank nonreligious ones, and exegesis, hadith, and jurisprudence all depend on theology’s establishment of the Creator, prophecy, and divine unity.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Third reason: theology is nobler because its opposites, unbelief and innovation, are among the vilest things.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Fourth reason: knowledge can be honored by its subject, need, or proof; astronomy illustrates noble subject, medicine greater need, and arithmetic stronger proofs, while theology combines all three.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Theology’s subject is exceptionally noble: it investigates God’s essence, attributes, acts, and the categories of what exists and does not exist.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Its religious need is great because knowing these matters earns immense reward and association with angels, while ignorance brings punishment and association with devils.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Its worldly need is great because social order depends on belief in the Creator and resurrection; without that belief, disorder would spread.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · قائلون | reports | Some also exempt slaves: the specific duty to obey their masters takes precedence over the general command to worship.
[RAZI-FULL:v2p79/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · القاضي | reports | Al-Qāḍī says the verse identifies God’s creation and beneficence as the reason worship exists.
